primary_secondary.note: Practitioner-researcher column on Google's own measurement approach; not a synthesis of other studies.

study_type.note: Claude adds 'position paper'; NotebookLM's 'mixed methods' describes Google's measurement practice (logs, diary studies, surveys), not the article's own design.

research_method.claude: Experience report / position column (version of a September 2024 keynote) on how Google's Engineering Productivity Research team measures productivity; no own empirical study
research_method.nlm: Experience report describing Google's logs-based metrics, diary studies and longitudinal quarterly surveys; invited column, no empirical tables or statistical testing
research_method.value: Experience report / invited IEEE Software column (version of a September 2024 keynote) describing Google's Engineering Productivity Research measurement approach: speed-ease-quality model, logs-based metrics validated against diary studies, longitudinal quarterly engineering survey; no new empirical data or analysis reported

context.claude: Industry; Google (mostly in-house developer tools); sample not reported (logs for approximately every engineer, quarterly survey, no numbers); also discusses small and medium organizations
context.nlm: Industry; Google; software engineers at Google (logs for approximately every engineer plus quarterly survey respondents)
context.value: industry; Google (Engineering Productivity Research team, mostly in-house developer tools); no sample size reported (logs cover approximately every engineer, plus quarterly survey)

space_applied.note: SPACE only referenced: Google's approach is 'similar to using frameworks like SPACE'.

ai_discussed.nlm: No (marks Yes, but its only basis is one sentence on adjusting the survey for AI)
ai_discussed.note: Single passing mention that the survey is being adjusted 'given how AI is changing developer experience and productivity'.

remote_covid.note: Both report work mode not specified; COVID-19 appears only as an example of always-on logs and survey agility (two bullet points).

data_window.note: Not stated by either (column, no analysed dataset).

cat_productivity.note: Speed outcome of the speed-ease-quality model (code delivered over time, iteration speed, self-reported velocity).

cat_quality.note: Quality outcome; test flakiness, technical debt (survey).

cat_collaboration.note: Code review appears only as a tradeoff example ('get rid of code review'), not as a metric.

cat_satisfaction.note: Overall role satisfaction and satisfaction with own velocity measured by survey.

cat_activity.note: Logs-based time usage and activity metrics, active coding time; LOC and changes submitted discussed critically.

cat_delivery.note: Thin basis: 'code delivered to production over time' as a speed measure and build latency, both labelled Delivery by the two extractors.

cat_devex.note: Flow (and NotebookLM's flow/focus/friction) is labelled DevEx by both, but cites Google's own flow work, not the Noda/Storey/Forsgren DevEx framework.

cat_survey.note: Longitudinal quarterly engineering satisfaction survey, self-reported productivity, diary studies.

evidence.quote: IN SEPTEMBER 2024, we gave a keynote address at the Developer Productivity Engineering Summit, in San Francisco, CA, USA. This article is a version of that talk.
At Google, most of our developer tools have been developed in-house, and most developers use the same set of tools.
evidence.loc: PDF p. 3 (Use Logs and Survey Data Together)

evidence.quote: We validate our logs-based metrics against self-reported data collected in diary studies with developers
evidence.loc: PDF p. 3 (Use Logs and Survey Data Together)

evidence.quote: We typically think of productivity as a balance among speed, ease, and quality.
evidence.loc: PDF p. 3 (Measure Speed, Ease, and Quality)

evidence.quote: in addition to measuring speed in terms of how much code is delivered to production over time, or how quickly developers are able to execute a single iteration of coding
Specifically, parsimony is an important consideration when one is designing a specific metric: “build latency,” “active coding time,” or “test flakiness.”
We use these logs to create metrics that measure developers’ time usage and activity.
when measuring engineering speed, some metrics (lines of code, changes submitted) emphasize the production of code specifically.
Our longitudinal quarterly engineering satisfaction survey asks engineers about a wide variety of topics related to developer productivity and satisfaction.
For example, we ask respondents about their overall satisfaction in their role
We ask about topics one might eventually measure objectively (“flow,” technical debt) in service of developing objective measures and getting some signal in the interim.
